meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It is too probable that no plan we propose will be adopted. Perhaps another dreadful conflict is to be sustained'?
meta.ogDescription: Its closing line is carved on the Washington Square Arch — but the whole passage is sourced to one funeral oration. What Morris printed in 1800, and why Lodge doubted it.

answer.label: Disputed — Washington as recalled by Gouverneur Morris
answer.authorDates: 1752–1816 · Constitutional Convention delegate; author of New York's official 1799 eulogy for Washington
answer.sourceLine: These sentences survive in exactly one place: Gouverneur Morris’s Oration, upon the Death of General Washington, delivered at New York on 31 December 1799 and printed there in 1800, where Morris presents them as Washington’s words spoken informally before the Federal Convention had even reached a quorum. James Madison’s Convention notes have nothing like them — Wikiquote records that they are absent from Madison’s summary of 25 May 1787 — and Henry Cabot Lodge concluded the wording was Morris’s own — while George Bancroft accepted the passage as genuine.

source.heading: The eulogy that is the only source

docMeta.dd: An Oration, upon the Death of General Washington
New York City, 31 December 1799, at the request of the Corporation of the City of New-York
New-York: printed by John Furman, opposite the City Hall, 1800 — passage at pp. 20–21

source.excerpt: AMERICANS! let the opinion then delivered by the greatest and best of men, be ever present to your remembrance. He was collected within himself. His countenance had more than usual solemnity — his eye was fixed, and seemed to look into futurity. “It is (said he) too probable that no plan we propose will be adopted. Perhaps another dreadful conflict is to be sustained. If to please the people, we offer what we ourselves disapprove, how can we afterwards defend our work? Let us raise a standard to which the wise and the honest can repair. The event is in the hand of God.” — This was the patriot voice of WASHINGTON; and this the constant tenor of his conduct.
trail: The words first appear in Gouverneur Morris's Oration, upon the Death of General Washington, printed at New-York by John Furman in 1800 ↗, pp. 20–21 — the eulogy Morris delivered on 31 December 1799.
Max Farrand reprinted the oration among the Convention's supplementary records; ConSource carries that text from The Records of the Federal Convention of 1787, vol. 3 (Yale University Press, 1911) ↗.

Wikiquote lists the passage under Disputed ↗, noting it was not recorded in Madison's summary of 25 May 1787, that George Bancroft accepted it as genuine, and that Henry Cabot Lodge gave reasons for rejecting it.

Lodge, George Washington, vol. II ↗ quotes the passage, judges in the main text that “the language is no doubt that of Morris,” and appends a footnote arguing from Madison's manuscript notes that Washington entered the Convention's debates only once.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the 1800 New-York printing; eighteenth-century typography normalised. Note what Morris says a few lines earlier: “It is a question, previous to the first meeting, what course shall be pursued” — he places the remark before the Convention convened, which is why no Convention record could contain it.

author.name: Gouverneur Morris
author.heading: The man who actually wrote the sentence
author.metaLine: 1752–1816 · Pennsylvania delegate to the Constitutional Convention · U.S. Minister to France, 1792–1794
author.bio: Gouverneur Morris sat on the Convention’s Committee of Style and Arrangement and is credited with the final wording of the Preamble — the change from “We, the People of the States” to “We, the People of the United States” — which earned him the nickname Penman of the Constitution. He later served as Minister Plenipotentiary to France. When Washington died, the Corporation of the City of New York asked Morris to deliver the city’s official eulogy, and it is that oration, not any Convention record, that gives us this quotation.

cite.sourceCitation: Gouverneur Morris, An Oration, upon the Death of General Washington, Delivered at the Request of the Corporation of the City of New-York, on the 31st Day of December, 1799 (New-York: Printed by John Furman, 1800), 20–21. Reprinted in Max Farrand, ed., The Records of the Federal Convention of 1787, vol. 3 (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1911). No source earlier than this oration is known.

misattribution.heading: How the quotation drifted
misattribution.intro: Nobody invented this line out of thin air — Morris was a delegate reporting a colleague. What has drifted is everything around the words: where they were said, who was presiding, and how they end.

items.why: The LOC's own reference book prints the passage as “remarks at the first Continental Congress, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, May 14, 1787” and adds “Washington was the presiding officer.” No body called the First Continental Congress was sitting in 1787 — the meeting in question was the Federal Convention. See entry 340 ↗.

Morris writes “He is their President” of a moment he simultaneously dates “previous to the first meeting.” Lodge points out the contradiction ↗: if Washington said this at all, he said it before the delegates had assembled and elected him.

items.who: John Fiske, The Critical Period of American History
items.why: Lodge records that Fiske “describes Washington as rising from his president's chair and addressing the convention with great solemnity” ↗ — and answers that there is “no authority whatever” for it.
The line is routinely served as “…the rest is in the hands of God,” as here ↗. The 1800 printing reads “The event is in the hand of God.”

items.who: Pages citing “the opening of the Convention, 25 May 1787”
items.why: Wikiquote notes the words were not recorded in Madison's summary of the events of 25 May 1787 ↗, and Lodge argues from Madison's manuscript that Washington entered the Convention's debates only once, over Gorham's amendment.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentiment may well be Washington's — Lodge allowed that Morris “no doubt” heard him urge it “frequently and forcibly” — but the sentence you can actually quote was written by Gouverneur Morris, for a funeral ↗.

context.heading: The waiting week in Philadelphia
lead: Washington reached Philadelphia on 13 May 1787, the day before the Convention was due to open, and a week went by before enough states arrived to make a quorum. In that idle week, Henry Cabot Lodge writes, there was “some informal discussion among the members present” ↗ between delegates who wanted an entirely new constitution and those who wanted only half-measures. Morris’s eulogy freezes one moment out of those unrecorded days.

The passage went on to become civic scripture — though what the stonemasons chose was its closing pair of sentences, not the opening lines this page is keyed to. “Let us raise a standard to which the wise and the honest can repair. The event is in the hand of God.” is carved across the attic of the Washington Square Arch in New York ↗, and Wikiquote records the passage engraved above the Fifteenth Street entrance to the Department of Commerce building and on a bronze plaque at Constitution Hall ↗ in Washington, D.C. — three permanent inscriptions resting on one eulogist’s memory.
context.detailsSummary: Lodge's case against the quotation, in three moves
detailsBody: Washington spoke once. Lodge cites Madison’s own bracketed note that when Washington took the floor for Gorham’s amendment “it was the only occasion on which the president entered at all into the discussions of the convention” — and says he examined the manuscript at the State Department himself.

Morris contradicts himself. The 1800 printing reads “He is their President. It is a question, previous to the first meeting, what course shall be pursued” (Lodge quotes it more loosely, as “previous to their first meeting”) — making Washington president before the delegates had met to elect him. Lodge calls this “a fair illustration of the loose and rhetorical character of the passage.”

The staging was invented later. Lodge notes that John Fiske described Washington rising from the president’s chair to address the Convention, and answers that there is “no authority whatever” for it. Lodge’s own verdict is generous but firm: the words are Morris’s presentation of a sentiment he had genuinely heard Washington press.
context.pull: The language is no doubt that of Morris, speaking from memory and in a highly rhetorical vein.
